anchors: Repeatedly misses agreed commitments without communicating risks, causing material disruption.
Meets commitments inconsistently and needs recurring intervention or late escalation.
Reliably delivers agreed work, tests it, and communicates risks with expected independence.
Sustains exceptional delivery impact beyond role expectations while improving team delivery practices.
answers: In week 2 the developer missed the agreed API integration deadline by two days, did not flag the blocker until I asked, and QA had to move the release test window.

In week 7 the developer again missed the agreed pagination delivery date by a day and needed my intervention to agree a smaller scope with product. They completed the reduced scope after that discussion.

anchors: Repeatedly obstructs shared engineering work or leaves material issues unresolved.
Collaboration is inconsistent and regularly needs intervention.
Provides timely, useful reviews and works constructively with peers on shared problems.
Consistently improves engineering effectiveness beyond normal peer expectations with demonstrable broader impact.
answers: In week 3 the developer reviewed my retry-handler pull request within our agreed review window, identified a duplicate-request bug, and supplied a reproducible test. I fixed it before release.

In week 8 the developer paired with me on a failing integration test, helped isolate a serialization mismatch, and documented the correction so the other service owner could apply it. We completed the agreed integration that day.

anchors: Repeatedly withholds necessary direction or support, preventing the reporting member from doing their work.
Provides inconsistent guidance or delegates without sufficient clarity and follow-through.
Sets clear expectations, gives useful feedback, and supports the reporting member in working independently.
Sustains development beyond ordinary supervision, with concrete growth in independent capability and wider reusable benefits.
answers: In week 4 the developer delegated a cache invalidation task to me with acceptance criteria, reviewed my design instead of taking over the implementation, and gave targeted feedback. I completed the task and explained the design tradeoffs independently in review.

In week 9 the developer helped me turn my troubleshooting notes into a guide used by two new engineers. I then resolved a similar production-like staging incident independently using the debugging approach they had taught me.
